articles.title: Ranking Member Maxine Waters and Committee Democrats Blast SEC Push to Eliminate Climate Risk Disclosures - House Financial Services Committee Democrats (.gov)
articles.summary: Ranking Member Maxine Waters and Committee Democrats Blast SEC Push to Eliminate Climate Risk Disclosures  House Financial Services Committee Democrats (.gov)
articles.full_text:
Today, Congresswoman Maxine Waters (D-CA), the top Democrat on the House Financial Services Committee, along with Representatives Nydia Velázquez (D-NY), Brad Sherman (D-CA), Gregory Meeks (D-NY), Stephen Lynch (D-MA), Al Green (D-TX), Emanuel Cleaver (D-MO), Bill Foster (D-IL), Joyce Beatty (D-OH), Juan Vargas (D-CA), Ayanna Pressley (D-MA), Rashida Tlaib (D-MI), Ritchie Torres (D-NY), Sylvia Garcia (D-TX), Nikema Williams (D-GA) and Sam Liccardo (D-CA), sent a letter to the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) Chairman Paul S. Atkins strongly opposing the Commission’s proposal to eliminate the March 2024 climate-related disclosure rules.
In the letter, the lawmakers warn that eliminating the rules would deprive investors of critical information about the financial risks companies face from climate change at a time when climate-related events are becoming increasingly more common and disruptive to businesses and the broader economy. They argue that the SEC has a responsibility to ensure investors have consistent, standardized information necessary to evaluate these risks and make informed decisions with their money.
“Stripping away these rules denies investors the information they need to accurately assess a company’s long-term value and to make sound, well-informed decisions with their hard-earned money,” the lawmakers wrote.
The lawmakers also dispute the Commission’s argument that the SEC exceeded its statutory authority in adopting the rules. They point to the SEC’s longstanding authority under federal securities laws to determine what information public companies must disclose to investors, as well as the Commission’s decades-long history of requiring disclosures in response to evolving market risks and economic conditions. The letter notes that the SEC has required various forms of environmental disclosure dating back to the 1970s and argues that climate-related disclosures fall within the Commission’s traditional role of ensuring investors have relevant information when making investment decisions.
The lawmakers added, “…nothing in the governing statutes, case law, or legislative history has changed since March 2024, and Congress has amended neither the Securities Act nor the Exchange Act. The only thing that has changed is the composition of the Commission.”
The letter also pushes back on arguments that climate disclosures are unnecessary or immaterial to investors. The lawmakers point to data showing that companies actively managing climate risks can realize significant financial benefits, while 80 percent of investors want the opportunity to invest in companies that consider environmental sustainability. Investors and financial institutions representing hundreds of trillions of dollars in assets have also sought climate-related information from companies to inform their investment and financing decisions.
The lawmakers conclude by urging the Commission to maintain the existing disclosure framework and withdraw its proposal to rescind the rules.
Full list of signers includes: Nydia Velázquez (D-NY), Brad Sherman (D-CA), Gregory Meeks (D-NY), Stephen Lynch (D-MA), Al Green (D-TX), Emanuel Cleaver (D-MO), Bill Foster (D-IL), Joyce Beatty (D-OH), Juan Vargas (D-CA), Ayanna Pressley (D-MA), Rashida Tlaib (D-MI), Ritchie Torres (D-NY), Sylvia Garcia (D-TX), Nikema Williams (D-GA), Sam Liccardo (D-CA).
Read the full letter HERE.
Background:
    - June 16, 2021 — Passed climate-risk disclosure legislation through the House. Then Chairwoman Waters led House passage of a broader ESG disclosure package, which would require public companies to disclose financial and business risks associated with climate change. Read Waters' floor statement on passage of the legislation. 
- March 21, 2022 — Applauded the SEC's proposed climate-disclosure rule after years of Committee action. Then-Chairwoman Waters joined committee Dems in a letter to commending the SEC's proposed rule requiring climate-related disclosures by public companies. Waters highlighted that, under her leadership, the Committee had already held four hearings on the issue and advanced legislation from Committee Democrats over the previous two Congresses. Read Waters and Committee Dems statement on the proposed SEC rule. 
- October 6, 2023 — Pressed SEC Chair Gary Gensler to quickly finalize the rule. Waters urged Gensler to finish the long-awaited climate-risk disclosure rule, warning that climate change and transition risks threatened Americans' investments, retirement savings, businesses and broader financial stability. She argued that investors needed consistent and comparable information to understand those risks. Read Waters' letter urging Gensler to finalize the climate-risk disclosure rule. 
- March 7, 2024 — Supported the SEC's final climate-disclosure rule while pushing for stronger protections. After the SEC finalized the rule, Waters welcomed the creation of standardized climate-risk disclosures but criticized the Commission for significantly weakening its original proposal. She specifically raised concerns about the treatment of Scope 1 and 2 emissions and the elimination of Scope 3 requirements, while emphasizing the real financial consequences of climate change for investors, homeowners and renters. Read Waters' statement on the final SEC climate-disclosure rule.
- April 10, 2024 — Defended the climate rule against Republican attacks in a full Committee hearing. At a Republican-led hearing titled “Beyond Scope: How the SEC's Climate Rule Threatens American Markets,” Waters defended the rule as a commonsense investor protection, arguing that climate change affects companies' financial health and investors have a right to understand how the companies they own are responding to those risks. Read Waters' opening statement defending the SEC climate rule. 
- June 5, 2024 — Led 36 lawmakers with Senator Elizabeth Warren in pressing the SEC to defend and enforce the rule. Waters and Warren led 36 lawmakers urging the SEC to remain focused on climate risk despite litigation challenging the rule. They called on the Commission to enforce its existing climate-risk guidance while the rule was stayed, use every available resource to defend the rule in court and robustly implement it once the stay was lifted. Read the Waters-Warren letter and Committee release. 
- September 17–19, 2024 — Fought Republican legislation restricting the SEC's disclosure authority. Waters opposed H.R. 4790, warning that it would restrict the SEC's authority to determine what information public companies must disclose, including environmental and climate-related information, and undermine investors' access to information about the companies they own. She testified against the legislation before the Rules Committee on September 17 and opposed it again on the House floor on September 19. Read Waters' September 17 testimony against H.R. 4790. Read Waters' September 19 floor statement. 
- December 29, 2025 — Demanded SEC oversight after Chairman Paul Atkins abandoned the climate-rule defense. Waters called for a long-overdue oversight hearing with Atkins amid sweeping changes at the SEC, including the Commission's retreat from climate-risk disclosure. The request put the Administration's reversal of climate-related investor protections squarely within the Committee Democrats' broader oversight of Atkins' leadership. Read Waters' request for an SEC oversight hearing. 
- February 11, 2026 — Confronted Atkins directly over halting the SEC's defense of the climate rule. When Atkins finally appeared before the Committee, Waters criticized his SEC for having “halted the SEC's defense of the climate disclosure rule” even as the California wildfires demonstrated the material financial risks associated with climate change. She placed the decision within a broader critique that Atkins' SEC was prioritizing Wall Street and billionaires over investors. Read Waters' February 2026 opening statement confronting Atkins.

articles.full_text:
SBTi Seeks Industry Input as It Revises FLAG Climate Standard
- SBTi is developing Version 2 of its Forest, Land and Agriculture Standard through a consultation and testing process expected to run for more than 12 months.
- More than 400 companies already have FLAG targets, while agriculture, forestry and land use remain the third-largest source of emissions after energy and industry.
- Companies should continue setting targets under the current FLAG Guidance, while applying new tools from the Corporate Net-Zero Standard V2 where relevant.
The Science Based Targets initiative is asking companies across agriculture, forestry and land-based supply chains to help reshape its climate target-setting framework.
SBTi has issued a call for evidence to support the development of Version 2 of its Forest, Land and Agriculture, or FLAG, Standard. The process will examine how companies are applying science-based targets across widely different markets, commodities and regulatory environments.
The initiative is particularly seeking participation from businesses in underrepresented regions central to global FLAG supply chains. Latin America and Southeast Asia are among the regions highlighted.
Companies can submit evidence or participate in virtual stakeholder meetings. The engagement will feed into a development process expected to last more than 12 months.
Corporate net-zero rules move into FLAG
The revision follows the publication of SBTi’s Corporate Net-Zero Standard V2 in June 2026. That framework introduced several changes to corporate target setting.
These include company categorization based on factors such as market, size and country. It also introduced five-year target review cycles and a broader range of target-setting options. A new hierarchy provides guidance on how companies should implement targets and deliver emissions reductions.
SBTi will now assess how those approaches could work for companies with significant land-related emissions.
Another priority is alignment with the Greenhouse Gas Protocol Land Sector and Removals Standard. Greater clarity between the two frameworks could prove important for companies navigating increasingly complex climate accounting requirements.
Businesses do not need to wait for the new FLAG Standard before setting targets. SBTi said companies should continue using the existing FLAG Guidance, Version 1.2.
Those companies can already apply key innovations from the Corporate Net-Zero Standard V2. These include the updated absolute contraction approach and the best-efforts framework for pursuing targets.
Agriculture faces mounting climate and transition risks
The revision comes as land-intensive businesses face a difficult operating environment. Costs are rising, regulatory requirements continue to evolve and investors are demanding stronger evidence of credible transition planning.
Climate exposure is also particularly acute across agriculture and forestry. Extreme weather can affect crop yields, commodity prices, supply availability and operating costs.
That combination makes FLAG emissions both a climate issue and a material business risk.
More than 400 companies have already established FLAG targets, according to SBTi. The next version of the framework will draw on their implementation experience alongside evidence from companies that have struggled with existing requirements.
RELATED ARTICLE: SBTi Publishes Draft Power Sector Net-Zero Framework
David Kennedy, Chief Executive Officer at the Science Based Targets initiative, said: “The FLAG sector has a key role in addressing the climate crisis. There has been much corporate activity in this space, with innovation and learning. With this call for evidence, companies can share their experience and shape an updated FLAG approach that will support farming transformation in the next phase of corporate climate action.”
“More than 400 companies already have FLAG targets and are managing transition risk, building long-term resilience, and meeting stakeholder and investor expectations. An updated FLAG approach that best reflects opportunities and challenges for corporate climate action will allow these companies and many more to progress on their journey. This will be good for business and make a vital contribution to achievement of international climate objectives.”
What executives and investors should watch
SBTi plans a structured development process under its 2026-2030 strategy and standards development procedures. It will incorporate implementation experience, stakeholder evidence, public consultations, pilot testing and expert working groups.
For companies, the process creates an opportunity to influence how future requirements handle complex supply chains, commodity exposure and regional differences.
For investors, the revision could affect how corporate land-sector targets are assessed and compared. Stronger alignment between SBTi and greenhouse gas accounting standards may also improve consistency in transition planning.
The stakes extend well beyond agricultural companies. FLAG supply chains run through food, retail, consumer goods and other global industries. How SBTi revises the framework will therefore shape how a broad group of companies manages land-related emissions, climate risk and long-term resilience.

articles.title: Brand expands community access to recycling services, designs packaging for circular economy - The Star
articles.summary: Brand expands community access to recycling services, designs packaging for circular economy  The Star
articles.full_text:
NESTLE Malaysia is stepping up its community recycling efforts with the launch of “Nestle Kitar”.
It is a refreshed platform building on its Project SAVE (Segregate, Avoid, Value, Educate) – the brand’s voluntary Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) initiative.
“Nestle Kitar” aims to expand community participation in recycling nationwide.
It will do so through enhanced collection services, recycling education and strategic partnerships, supporting Malaysia’s transition towards a more circular economy, the company said in a media statement.
The initiative was introduced at the “Nestle: Sustainability, Connected” event in Petaling Jaya, Selangor, which was launched by Deputy Natural Resources and Environmental Sustainability Minister Syed Ibrahim Syed Nohat.
Also present were Nestle S.A. assistant vice-president and head of sustainability for Asia, Oceania and Africa Katarzyna Grzybowska, alongside representatives from government agencies, industry partners and civil society organisations.
Nestle Malaysia chief executive officer Juan Aranols said Malaysia generated an estimated 40,000 tonnes of solid waste every day.
A significant proportion comprised materials that could potentially be recycled.
“This underlines the importance of making recycling more accessible and strengthening separation at source.
“‘Nestle Kitar’ is a critical part of how we deliver on our global vision that none of our packaging ends up in landfill or as litter.
“Reduced use of plastics and better packaging design are necessary blocks to build a circular economy.
“Additionally, we must also strengthen collection and recovery through effective recycling systems, community participation and strong partnerships,” he said.
Aranols said Project SAVE had laid the foundation over the past six years.
“Through ‘Nestle Kitar’, we will now further build on this progress to reach more households and help make responsible recycling practices part of everyday life,” he said.
Since its establishment in 2020, Project SAVE had grown to serve about 270,000 households across nine cities, providing regular household recycling collection and encouraging separation at source.
To date, the programme had recovered and recycled 50,000 tonnes of dry mixed recyclables, including 32,000 tonnes of plastics.
According to the company, “Nestle Kitar” reflected the collective effort required to build a more effective recycling ecosystem.
It embodied a shared responsibility among industry, government agencies, local authorities, waste management concessionaires, recyclers and communities to expand collection services, reduce waste, strengthen recycling education and encourage consistent household participation.
The platform also complemented the company’s broader efforts to reduce virgin plastic, increase the use of recycled materials, and design packaging for recyclability.
As of 2025, 95.6% of Nestle Malaysia’s packaging was designed for recycling, building on pioneering innovations.
This included the introduction of high-quality recycled plastic resin (rPET) bottles across its Ready-to-Drink beverage portfolio – a first in Malaysia – as well as replacing plastic bowls and cups with sustainable paper-based alternatives across selected product categories.
According to the statement, the company was also the first in Malaysia to transition to 100% paper straws across its entire UHT range, helping eliminate more than 1.2 billion plastic straws from the environment to date.

articles.title: Estonia takes lead on circular economy policy - World Bio Market Insights
articles.summary: Estonia takes lead on circular economy policy  World Bio Market Insights
articles.full_text:
Estonia has become one of the most circular countries in the world.
In 2025, the Baltic nation placed 3rd in Sensoneo’s global waste management ranking – up from 32nd just three years prior.
Its rapid ascent owed to a suite of new waste management policies, as well as ambitious circular roadmaps and targets.
How has Estonia taken control of its circular economy in such a rapid space of time? And what can other economies learn from it?
A tale of one city
Estonia’s recent achievements in waste management owes a lot to policy initiatives in its capital city, Tallinn.
Here, where medieval turrets pierce the skyline, the local government has brought out pioneering policies to spur the circular economy.
In October 2019, Tallinn brought in a local anti-plastic regulation banning single-use tableware completely at public events. The new rules said that only reusable alternatives could be used. The aim was to change the behaviour of both businesses and food consumers, cutting waste at the supply and consumption end simultaneously.
Even before then, the city was already the national leader in sustainable waste management. Biowaste collection there almost tripled between 2012 and 2019. Landfill decreased by 70% over the same period. On any measure, the city was leaps and bounds ahead of other global cities when it came to waste progress.
National government takes notice
Over the 2002s, Tallinn’s circular activities began impacting national policymaking. The city’s success in tackling waste convinced central lawmakers that a bigger circular overhaul nationwide might just be possible.
Emulating Tallinn’s success at a national level, Estonia became the first EU member state to mandate the exclusive use of reusable containers and cutlery at all public events nationwide, regardless of the number of guests. The law came into force as of 1 January 2024.
The country also has a wider circular vision beyond single-use plastics. The Estonian government’s 2022 “Estonia 2035” strategy says that it aims for a 30% national circular material use rate target by 2035, up from 17% in 2020. This exceeds the EU’s 2030 circular material use rate target (24%), as well as the current EU rate (around 12.2%).
Tallinn’s circular ambitions
When it comes to circular ambitions, Estonia’s capital is just getting started.
The city’s Circular Economy Development Plan 2035 explicitly links circularity to the city’s carbon emissions goals. Its aim is for the circular economy sector to reduce the city’s carbon emissions by 40% compared to 2007.
The plan also seeks to increase the city’s share of recycled materials to over 65%, while reducing the share of landfilled waste.
Tallinn is not going it alone in this. In 2025, the city successfully applied to become a Zero Waste Candidate City, a certification awarded by the Mission Zero Academy. As part of the programme, Mission Zero Academy will help Tallinn along with its ambitious goals.
The city is also vying to make an impact internationally. It participates in the international partnership aimed at developing green cities, the Greener Cities partnership program, implemented jointly by the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) and the United Nations Human Settlements Programme (UN-Habitat).
Tallinn is part of a global trend whereby cities are leading on major circular policy. Urban areas are becoming laboratories for the most innovative circular policy experimentation, trialling schemes that could be rolled out elsewhere.
More nimble on its feet than national legislatures, and enjoying the backing of climate-conscious urban citizens, city administrations can often deliver innovative policies quicker than central government.
National policies through local means
Tallinn’s leadership on circular issues has convinced the government that other local authorities in Estonia should be brought on board with regards to circular policies.
Regions differ in population and basic resources, meaning they have different roles to play in advancing the circular economy. To scope local conditions, the government initiated its 2023 project “Enhancing Circular Economy Capacity in Local Governments”.
The project saw Estonian municipalities, in collaboration with the TalTech research group, prepare their own circular economy roadmaps. 79 roadmaps resulted from the initiative.
The scoping exercise revealed that the most important way for municipal authorities to participate in building circularity is by ramping up public engagement and communication around green policy.
Being closer to actual citizens, local governments are often the most effective channel for encouraging the public campaigns to rescue and re-use waste.
Ultimately, local authorities need strong regulation from the central government to roll out serious initiatives.
However, locally-run public engagement campaigns can determine the success of circular initiatives, winning public support and locking in momentum for the long-term.
Waste management lays the foundations
All circular economies depend on robust waste management. Without high rates of collection and sorting, usable waste materials disappear into incineration or landfills, making upcycling impossible.
Effective waste systems do two things: cut unnecessary waste and ensure any re-usable materials keep circulating through the economy.
Estonia’s new waste management laws aim to do both. In 2026, the government brought a new Waste Law into force, containing rules that will affect residents, waste collectors, the state, and municipal authorities.
Included were new penalties designed to cut waste such as higher landfill fees and a new fee for incinerating waste. It also sets a target for municipal authorities to separate and collect 67% of its waste by 2027.
Lawmakers are already pushing for more stringent waste management rules. In June 2026 the Ministry of Climate sent a Waste Act draft amendment for approval targeting food and textile waste in particular.
Under the draft law, large retail, wholesale and manufacturing companies will be required to measure the amount of food waste they generate and develop plans to reduce it. They must also expand food donation and redistribution and companies will be required to cooperate with at least one food‑redistribution organization.
The textile component of the amendment is designed to fulfil EU-wide laws cracking down on fast fashion waste. The principle is to make producers, rather than consumers, pay for collection and recycling, something that Estonia plans to introduce by 2028.
Old waste, new materials
With waste management locked in, the final piece of the circular puzzle is building infrastructure that can upcycle waste.
Estonia is not short on waste valorisation R&D. Native startups are already being enlisted by the government in its waste reduction drive.
The Estonian government has pumped nearly €2M in funding for Äio and TFTAK to build a digital biomanufacturing platform that can turn food and wood industry waste into planet-friendly fats.
EU support is also helping domestic waste firms scale. The EU Just Transition Fund put €39 million into a €100 million textile recycling and manufacturing complex in the northeast, set to be the largest of its kind in the Nordic region with an annual processing capacity of 70, 000.
Going outside the city
Many of Estonia’s circular policies have centred around managing municipal waste – household and business waste.
However, agro-waste also has a key role to play in developing Estonia’s circular economy.
In 2023, the Ministry of Regional Affairs and Agriculture released a national roadmap for valorising bio-resources including agro-waste.
Known as the Circular Bioeconomy Roadmap, the document lays out what the country must do in order to better valorise its domestic bio-resources, including increased R&D, changes to value chains and business models, and structural changes in land use. It urges particular emphasis on building high value sectors where basic raw materials are processed into more valuable items.
Meeting climate targets is just one purpose of a circular bioeconomy, according to the Roadmap. Upcycling waste also reduces dependence on imported resources among farmers, increasing the country’s food security.
Yet the Roadmap also suggests the Estonian government recognises the security benefits of circularity are not separate from its sustainability advantages. Using agro-waste to make circular farming inputs, for example, can help cut carbon emissions as well as displacing imports.
Making the circular transition appealing from multiple perspectives makes it more likely that these policies will gain consensus support from diverse stakeholders, giving circular policies staying power.
Why Estonia
Estonia has come a long way on circularity in a short period.
The country’s ambitious national goals are just one part of this. More importantly, the government has brought in a series of enforceable waste management regulations that cut waste and divert materials from landfill.
Estonia’s waste management policies are multi-faceted, tackling waste reduction, waste management, and waste valorisation at the same time. This reflects the government’s appreciation of the complex logistical issues involved in growing the circular economy.
Another strength of Estonia’s circular leadership has been the importance accorded to local authorities. Tallinn has led the way on this, inspiring central government efforts to get other local regions involved in shaping and implementing national policy.
What Estonia must do now is coordinate local and central government activities more effectively. It will have to find ways of getting local governments to act in ways that systematically advance national targets on circular material reuse.

articles.title: Working together towards a circular economy - Region of Durham
articles.summary: Working together towards a circular economy  Region of Durham
articles.full_text:
Circular Economy Month
Every year in October, we recognize Circular Economy Month to highlight the importance of reducing waste and making better use of our resources. A circular economy is a model that retains and recovers as much value as possible from resources by reusing, repairing, refurbishing, remanufacturing, or repurposing products and materials to maximize their value before they are recycled or thrown out.
Five material types have been identified as the priorities for reducing waste in Canada: Construction, Renovation, and Demolition, Textiles, Electronic and Critical Minerals, Packaging, and Food.
In recognition of Circular Economy Month, residents and the Region give examples of how we are reducing the amount of waste from these materials.
Construction waste
Construction activities generate nearly one-third of all solid waste in Canada, producing over four million tonnes of waste each year.
Uxbridge resident Melanie used wood from her home renovations for garden boxes, ensuring it did not go to waste. "When we renovated our home, we had leftover wood, including some reclaimed wood, that could have gone to a waste management facility,” said Melanie. “Instead, we saved it for future projects. This year, we used some of it to build garden boxes and we're planning to make a family name sign this fall. Sustainability is important to me, and reusing materials not only reduces waste, but it also saves money."
The Region is doing their part by piloting various technologies for cutting down on road construction waste, such as Hot in Place Recycling. With this process, the volume of aggregate materials, typically mined and trucked in for road construction, are significantly reduced, thereby lowering costs and reducing the environmental impact. No pavement waste was generated during the pilot, as all existing aggregates and asphalt cement were fully recovered and reused. This innovative project has been recognized with two awards—the Ontario Public Works Associations Award for Transportation Project of the Year in the less than $2M division and the 2025 Good Roads Municipal Paving Project of the Year Award.
Textiles
Canadians, on average, purchase 70 new articles of clothing a year, but only wear about 50 per cent of the clothes we own. Canadians throw out nearly 500 million kilograms (or about a billion pounds) of clothing and fabric-containing home goods every year.
Whitby resident Joyce visits local thrift stores regularly to keep her wardrobe updated. “You can find so many clothes that look brand new at a fraction of the price,” said Joyce. “When I no longer need them, I donate the clothes in good condition back to the thrift stores or to family members and friends.” To keep her clothes looking new longer, she uses her sewing skills to repair any small rips or tears, and air dries her clothes whenever possible rather than using a clothes dryer.
The Region also holds Environment Days throughout the year during which residents can drop off clothing and textiles in good condition, as well as other items, to then be donated to charities. Residents can also donate items in the marked donation bins at our waste management facilities.
Electronic waste
In 2022, the world produced a record 62 billion kilograms of electronic waste (e-waste), up 82 per cent from 2010. Electronic waste includes unwanted devices and cables, plus batteries and fluorescent lights. Nearly everything inside of them can be recovered and made into new products, however e-waste is growing five times faster than recycling rates.
When Ajax resident Maddie built her gaming computer, she bought refurbished parts found on Facebook Marketplace. “I was able to find a refurbished motherboard, graphics card and RAM,” said Maddie. “Buying refurbished instead of new saved me a significant amount of money.”
E-waste is accepted at the Region’s Environment Days as well, while bi-annual curbside battery collection is offered to residents for household batteries so they can be recycled. Durham residents can also drop off e-waste, including batteries, for recycling at our waste management facilities free of charge all year around. E-waste can also be collected at the curb by booking a special collection.
Packaging waste
Approximately 40 per cent of the plastic produced each year is packaging, used once and thrown away. Recycling one tonne of plastics prevents up to two tonnes of carbon pollution.
Bowmanville resident Jeff cuts down on packaging for his family by buying snacks in bulk instead of individual portions, or making their own snacks at home, such as trail mix and granola bars. The snacks are then put into reusable containers for work and school lunches.
In addition to supporting the recycling of plastics through the Blue Box program managed by Circular Materials, Durham Region also processes all green bin materials at an existing Anaerobic Digestion facility. This allowed the Region to expand the Green Bin program to include some products that contain a mix of plastics and compostable materials, such as diapers and menstrual products. Regional facilities also have water bottle filling stations to encourage staff to bring refillable water bottles to work.
Food waste
One-fifth, or 19 per cent, of all food produced in the world is lost or wasted every year, due in large part to household food waste practices.
Oshawa resident Stephanie gets creative with leftovers by turning them into a new meal to waste less. “Yesterday’s chicken is great in a quesadilla; a Sunday roast makes quick Monday night sliders; overripe bananas become freshly baked banana bread; and ripe fruit gets a second life in a smoothie,” said Stephanie.
The Region helps residents cut back on their daily food waste by offering tips on how to plan meals, store food and get creative with leftovers, so edible food doesn’t end up wasted. For food scraps that can be composted at home for use in the garden, backyard composters are available for residents to purchase online using the Region’s home delivery service.
The future of waste management
Even small changes in how we deal with waste daily can help us drastically reduce our carbon footprint and recover as much value as possible from resources. Throughout the year, the Region supports residents in their waste reduction efforts by promoting the five “Rs” (Rethink, Reduce, Reuse, Recycle, and Recover). In a perfect circular economy, nothing is wasted.
For more information about Durham’s waste collection programs, visit durham.ca/Waste.

articles.full_text:
Sponsors, industry partners, policymakers, brand owners, recyclers and certification specialists converge at CMT’s 22nd LAPET Series in Mexico City.
MEXICO CITY, MEXICO, October 6, 2026 /EINPresswire.com/ -- Latin America’s transition from a linear to a circular plastics economy is moving the packaging discussion beyond commitments and towards the practical questions of regulation, recycled-material supply, infrastructure, traceability, and commercial-scale technology. Centre for Management Technology (CMT) will convene the 22nd LAPET Series – Circular Plastics Packaging LATAM on 28–29 October 2026 at the Mexico City Marriott Reforma Hotel, showcasing industry players’ discussion on “Regulation to Reality: Delivering Circular Packaging Across Latin America.”
The event takes place as circular economy regulations, recycled-content commitments and investment in recycling infrastructure reshape packaging decisions across the region. Mexico’s Circular Economy legislation features prominently, with discussions focused on producer responsibility, recyclability, recycled-material availability and stronger circular value chains.
Supporting the conference are Alpek Polyester Mexico as the Gold & Networking Reception Sponsor, EREMA Group and Avient as Associate Sponsors, while ExxonMobil Signature Polymers joins as Coffee Break Reception Sponsor. Exhibitors include Alpek Polyester Mexico & Avient, bringing additional focus to material innovation and practical packaging solutions.
The discussion begins with Mexico’s Circular Economy Law and the readiness of the country’s plastics, packaging and recycling markets. Mayra Hernandez Navarro, Director of Government and Regulatory Affairs at ECOCE A.C.; Luz Elena Aristizábal Alviar, Community Relations, Public Affairs Leader LATAM at Essity; Dr. German Ruiz Mendez, Director General of Urban Environmental Development and Performance at the Ministry of Environment and Natural Resources (SEMARNAT); and Eduardo Solano, Circular Economy Consultant at NSM Ecosistemas Circulares, will join the discussion on implementation, EPR obligations, recycled-content compliance, collection readiness and investment needs.

Brand owners will examine how evolving regulation, packaging design, procurement priorities and market expectations are shaping future packaging portfolios. articles.title: Hong Kong Issues Record $2.6 Billion Digital Green Bond - ESG Today
articles.summary: Hong Kong Issues Record $2.6 Billion Digital Green Bond  ESG Today
articles.full_text:
The Government of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region of the People’s Republic of China (HKSAR) announced the pricing of approximately HK$20 billion (USD$2.6 billion) of digital green bonds, setting a new record for the largest-ever digital bond issuance in the world to date.
A digital green bond, or a tokenized green bond, is a green bond that is represented on a blockchain network. Investors trade the bonds on the blockchain-based exchange and principal and interest are paid on the blockchain. Digital bonds offer benefits including increased transparency and traceability, as well as faster transactions and settlements.
The offering included four tranches, denominated in currencies including HK dollars, Renminbi, US dollars, and euro.
According to the HKSAR Government, demand for the bonds was strong, with subscription ratios across the four currencies reaching 1.3 to 11.3 times.
The offering marks the fourth in a series of digital green bond issuances by the HKSAR Government, following an initial HK$800 million tokenized green bond issuance in early 2023, a second HK$6 billion issuance in 2024, and a third HK$10 billion issuance in November 2025.
The government highlighted an innovative feature of the fourth offering, under which tokenised deposits were incorporated into the primary issuance settlement process for the HKD tranche.
Mr Eddie Yue, the Chief Executive of the Hong Kong Monetary Authority, said:
“This fourth issuance reinforces our commitment to stay ahead in the digital finance space, continues to unlock new synergies across digital infrastructures, and deepens our digital asset ecosystem.”

The European Commission has launched a new €230 million research and innovation call under Horizon Europe
Published on 2 October by the Directorate-General for Research and Innovation (DG RTD), the call supports the European Union’s priorities on food security, water, nature and sustainable prosperity.
Supporting biodiversity research across Europe
The funding will increase investment in biodiversity research and innovation across Pillar II of Horizon Europe’s 2026–2027 Work Programme. It will also support research into the cause of biodiversity decline and practical solutions that can help ecosystems recover and become more resilient.
Ten areas of research
Some priorities include research into the effects of PFAS, or per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, on biodiversity and ecosystem services. Other topics will examine how clean and digital industries can affect biodiversity and explore ways to ensure their development delivers greater environmental benefits.
The programme will also support systemic approaches to accelerating transformative change for biodiversity, research into the drivers of invertebrate decline and new approaches to ecosystem restoration.
Living labs will also play an important role, with funding available to co-create restoration solutions, overcome implementation barriers, and improve resilience to environmental risks.
Other areas include developing innovative approaches to combat wildlife trafficking and invasive alien species, creating cost-effective biodiversity monitoring systems and advancing data-driven research at the biodiversity and health interface through a One Health approach.
The final topic focuses on strengthening the Global Ocean Observing System to support climate resilience, biodiversity conservation and Europe’s strategic autonomy.
Opportunities for potential applicants
The call will be presented during the Horizon Europe Horizontal Activities info day on 16 October 2026. The online event will cover the policy objectives behind the call, the topics available for applications, and key considerations around project design, impact, and implementation.
Participants will also have opportunities to ask questions through interactive Q&A sessions.
Researchers and organisations looking for potential collaborators can also take part in a Nature call brokerage event on 19 October, organised by the CARE4BIO project and the Cluster 6 National Contact Points network.
With €230 million available, the call offers a major opportunity for European research organisations and partners to develop practical solutions to protect biodiversity and build more resilient ecosystems.

articles.title: The EUDR is on the horizon – could it change again? - FoodNavigator.com
articles.summary: The EUDR is on the horizon – could it change again?  FoodNavigator.com
articles.full_text:
EUDR implementation briefing
- EUDR compliance begins in December 2026 for larger companies
- Further EUDR simplifications appear unlikely despite continued political opposition
- Industry support remains strong, though some companies seek changes
- A third delay remains possible but implementation appears more likely
- Further delays could undermine EUDR and EU credibility
The European Union Deforestation Regulation (EUDR) is on the horizon.
The deadline is fast approaching: larger companies will need to comply with the law from 30 December 2026, with the deadline for smaller companies coming six months later on 30 June 2027.
The law has seen two delays and several simplifications since it was first proposed.
Now that we’re on the home stretch, what are the chances that the landmark regulation will see last-minute changes, alterations or delays? Will it get over the line as planned?
The state of the EUDR
The EUDR has been through many shifts. In 2024, the regulation was delayed, which was followed in 2025 by a second year-long delay. Then, earlier this year, a simplification package was released, easing compliance burdens for certain operators.
Yet in the view of Bill Cordingley, barrister at the law firm Browne Jacobson, we have now arrived at the “definitive version” of the EUDR, or at least close to it.
“The Commission has already implemented a substantial simplification exercise and argues that, as a result, compliance costs have been significantly reduced.”
If there are any further changes, he suggests, they are more likely to focus on practical implementation issues, guidance and administrative burdens, rather than reworking the traceability and due diligence requirements themselves.
Further simplifications are “unlikely”, suggests Nicole Polsterer, sustainable consumption and production campaigner at the NGO Fern. Fern is not aware of a sizeable group within the European Parliament pushing for more simplifications.
Opposition to the EUDR from industry
The industry is broadly supportive of the EUDR, with companies such as Barry Callebaut and Ferrero backing the regulation.
However, opposition has been voiced from some quarters, with snacking giant Mondelēz International and coffee company Lavazza traditionally expressing concerns about the practicalities of the regulation.
According to the NGO Global Witness, Mondelēz has been lobbying the US government, with CEO Dirk Van de Put meeting US Ambassador to the EU Andrew Puzder to push to weaken the law.
According to Global Witness, Mondelēz has also been executing a “pan-European lobbying strategy”, targeting conservative MEPs in Brussels as well as meeting with governments in France, Germany, Ireland and Luxembourg.
In response to Global Witness’s piece, a Mondelēz spokesperson said that the company “fully supports the objectives of the EU Deforestation Regulation and remains committed to deforestation-free supply chains and responsible sourcing across our operations and value chain”.
Opposition to the EUDR from governments
The EUDR also faces opposition from the US, with Puzder describing it as “textbook overregulation”, which will “impose significant regulatory compliance costs while producing inconsequential environmental benefit”.
The US has asked for further simplifications for low-risk countries, explains Fern’s Polsterer.
Yet Browne Jacobson’s Cordingley does not believe that, at this stage, opposition from the US could lead to further changes. On the one hand, “external political pressures could still have some influence on the debate”, and concerns from trading partners such as the US could reinforce existing trends towards deregulation and attempts to rejuvenate competitiveness.
On the other, “the EUDR remains one of the EU’s flagship environmental measures and is not far off coming into force and so I do not think pressure from climate-sceptical governments alone is likely to be enough to derail it altogether”.
Opposition to the EUDR from the European Parliament
Then there is opposition from within the European Parliament. Groups such as the centre-right European People’s Party (EPP) have long been in favour of simplifications and revisions to the EUDR.
“Internally we know there is now a sizeable political constituency within the Parliament that would weaken parts of the regulation given the opportunity,” says Cordingley.
Yet a substantial coalition of MEPs still back the regulation and oppose any significant rollback. While Cordingley sees the potential for some pressure to further moderate the rules, he does not believe that there is an obvious Parliamentary majority to dismantle the regime entirely.
Could there be a third delay?
It would be “foolish” to rule out the possibility of a third delay, says Cordingley. EU Member States are still lobbying for further simplification and postponement. Political resistance has far from disappeared.
At the same time, the European Commission has presented the simplification package as addressing the concerns of industry and Member States, he says. It has repeatedly stressed the current timetable.
“I think implementation in December 2026 remains more likely than another delay but I can’t fully discount the political picture shifting quickly in the weeks ahead.”
How could further simplifications impact the law?
If more changes were introduced to the law, it would significantly weaken its credibility, suggests Tina Schneider, director of forest governance and policy at the organisation World Resources Institute (WRI).
“Moving the goalposts again would undermine confidence in the regulatory process and raise serious questions about the EU’s commitment to delivering on the environmental goals the law was designed to achieve.”
A third delay would weaken the credibility not only of the EUDR but of the EU itself, says Fern’s Polsterer. She suggests that if there is a delay, it may be blamed on the IT system or on food security.
Right now, things are looking good for the EUDR. But in the past, events have moved quickly. While opposition to the regulation remains, further simplifications, or even a further delay, cannot be completely ruled out.

articles.full_text:
Amazon Signs 36 MW Shetland Wind Deal to Expand UK Clean Energy Supply
- Amazon signed a 36 MW power purchase agreement with Statkraft for the Mossy Hill wind farm in Scotland’s Shetland Islands.
- The project is expected online in November 2030 and could generate electricity equivalent to the annual needs of more than 57,000 homes.
- Amazon has backed more than 50 carbon-free energy projects across the UK, with over 1 GW of combined capacity.
Amazon has signed a 36 MW power purchase agreement with Statkraft for a new wind farm in the Shetland Islands. The deal expands the technology group’s renewable electricity portfolio as it works toward net-zero carbon across its operations by 2040.
The Mossy Hill wind farm, located near Lerwick, is expected to begin operating in November 2030. Once operational, it is projected to generate enough electricity to match the annual consumption of more than 57,000 homes.
For Statkraft, the long-term corporate agreement provides greater revenue certainty for the project. For Amazon, it adds another contracted renewable power source to a growing portfolio across Scotland and the wider UK.
Amazon Expands UK Renewable Energy Portfolio
The agreement builds on Amazon’s existing Scottish energy commitments. These include power purchase agreements linked to the Moray West offshore wind farm in the Moray Firth and Chirmorie Wind Farm in South Ayrshire.
The Chirmorie agreement is the UK’s largest onshore wind PPA.
John Boumphrey, Amazon UK and Ireland country manager, said: “Our latest project in the Shetland Islands builds on years of investment in renewable energy across the UK. From the Shetland Islands to the coasts of England, our renewable energy investments are creating real jobs and powering local communities. Last year we announced our plan to invest £40 billion in the UK by 2027, and the transition to a lower-carbon economy is a part of how we’re putting that commitment to work.”
Amazon’s previously announced UK investment plan is equivalent to approximately $54 billion.
The company has now invested in more than 50 carbon-free energy projects across the UK. Its wind and solar portfolio totals more than 1 GW of capacity. Amazon says that is enough electricity to match the annual consumption of more than 1.3 million UK households.
Corporate PPAs Support Project Financing
Long-term PPAs have become an important financing mechanism for renewable developers. They provide contracted demand while giving corporate buyers greater visibility over their electricity sourcing and decarbonization strategies.
Kevin O’Donovan, Statkraft’s UK and Ireland country manager, said: “We’re pleased to have agreed a partnership with Amazon for our Mossy Hill Wind Farm in Shetland, which gives us the certainty to move the project forward. Shetland has a proud history of energy production, and as the country shifts towards more homegrown renewable power, we’re proud to be playing our part in that transition.”
The agreement also comes as the UK seeks to expand domestic renewable generation and reduce its exposure to volatile fossil fuel markets. Scotland remains central to that effort because of its substantial wind resources and established energy infrastructure.
RELATED ARTICLE: Amazon Adds 50+ Mercedes Electric Trucks in Germany
Amazon has been the UK’s largest corporate purchaser of carbon-free energy for five consecutive years, according to BloombergNEF.
Its low-carbon investments in the country have exceeded approximately $4 billion. Analysis by Frontier Economics estimates those investments supported up to 34,000 jobs between 2021 and 2025. They also contributed up to roughly $2.7 billion in gross value added over the period.
European Clean Energy Portfolio Passes 10 GW
The Shetland agreement forms part of a much larger European procurement strategy.
Amazon has invested in more than 260 carbon-free energy projects across Europe. Together, they represent more than 10 GW of capacity.
Those investments support Amazon’s commitment under The Climate Pledge to reach net-zero carbon across its operations by 2040.
For executives and investors, Mossy Hill also illustrates the continuing role of corporate PPAs in bringing renewable projects toward construction. Large electricity buyers can provide developers with long-term revenue certainty while securing additional clean power for expanding operations.
In the UK, that relationship is becoming increasingly important as electricity demand rises and policymakers pursue greater energy security. Amazon’s latest agreement places Shetland within that corporate procurement landscape, connecting the islands’ wind resources with the decarbonization plans of one of the world’s largest electricity buyers.

Schneider Electric Appoints Lena Henry to Lead Global Sustainability Advisory Business
- Schneider Electric has appointed Lena Henry to lead SE Advisory Services, its global consulting practice focused on energy, sustainability and infrastructure transformation.
- Henry takes over as companies face mounting pressure to align growth, energy security, resilience and decarbonization with measurable financial outcomes.
- Thousands of organizations use the advisory business for energy procurement, renewable energy, climate risk, supply chain decarbonization and sustainability strategy.
Schneider Electric has appointed Lena Henry to lead its global advisory business as corporate demand grows for practical support on energy, sustainability and resilience.
Henry became Head of Advisory Services on September 1, 2026. She will oversee the growth strategy of SE Advisory Services, Schneider Electric’s global consulting practice.
Her mandate centers on helping companies convert sustainability and business objectives into measurable results. The practice combines strategic advice, technology and implementation across energy and infrastructure.
“Organizations are navigating profound changes across energy, sustainability, resilience, and digital transformation,” said Henry. “The challenge for many leaders is no longer defining ambition. It’s turning ambition into action and measurable results.”
Leadership change as sustainability priorities evolve
Henry succeeds Steve Wilhite, who is leaving Schneider Electric after a 25-year tenure. Wilhite previously served as president and CEO of Summit Energy before Schneider Electric acquired the business in 2011.
The leadership transition comes as sustainability strategies face greater scrutiny from boards, investors and regulators. Companies are increasingly expected to demonstrate how climate commitments translate into operational improvements, resilience and long-term value.
For Schneider Electric, that environment creates a growing market for advisory services that bridge corporate strategy and implementation.
“We help clients navigate complexity with confidence by combining world-class expertise, innovative technology, and practical execution that delivers real business value. I am honored to lead this exceptional team and excited about what we will accomplish together,” Henry said.
Schneider Electric launched SE Advisory Services in 2025 as its flagship global consulting practice. Its remit spans energy efficiency, sustainability and technology, with electrification, automation and digitalization central to its approach.
The business also advises companies on decarbonization, circularity and governance related to infrastructure modernization.
From climate targets to implementation
Thousands of organizations now use SE Advisory Services across several areas. These include energy procurement, renewable energy strategies, climate risk management, supply chain decarbonization, sustainability strategy and infrastructure transformation.
Its work increasingly reaches beyond companies’ direct operations.
The advisory business recently collaborated with Levi Strauss & Co. and Marks & Spencer on an initiative designed to help fashion suppliers adopt renewable electricity at scale. Such programs address a persistent corporate climate challenge: reducing emissions across complex global supply chains.
RELATED ARTICLE: Schneider Electric Backs New Climate Impact Framework
For large companies, Scope 3 emissions can sit outside direct operational control. Supplier engagement, renewable electricity procurement and financing structures therefore play a growing role in corporate transition plans.
“The future of our business is incredibly bright,” Henry added. “We have, exceptional people, trusted and enduring client relationships, and a market that increasingly needs what we do best.”
Operational experience shapes advisory strategy
Henry joined Schneider Electric in 2023 as a senior vice president responsible for global distribution and e-commerce operations. She most recently led global customer experience and commercial transformation.
Her career combines consulting with corporate operating roles. Before joining Schneider Electric, she spent more than a decade at McKinsey & Company and held senior leadership positions at EssilorLuxottica and in the home appliance sector.
That background gives Henry experience on both sides of the advisory relationship. She has worked on customer experience, new commercial models and the execution of corporate strategy.
For executives and investors, the appointment reflects a broader shift in the sustainability market. Corporate climate strategies are moving deeper into procurement, infrastructure, supply chains and capital planning.
The next phase will be judged less by the ambition of corporate targets and more by delivery. As energy volatility, climate risk and infrastructure requirements converge, advisory firms are competing to turn sustainability commitments into operational and financial outcomes.
Schneider Electric is positioning SE Advisory Services at that intersection, with Henry now responsible for translating growing demand into the practice’s next phase of global expansion.

articles.summary:
Equinor has appointed environmental consultancy ERM and law firm CMS to support development of its planned 1.5 GW offshore wind project in the Celtic Sea. The appointments will cover environmental […]
The post Equinor Advances 1.5 GW Celtic Sea Offshore Wind Project With ERM, CMS appeared first on ESG News.
articles.full_text:
Equinor Advances 1.5 GW Celtic Sea Offshore Wind Project With ERM, CMS
- Equinor has appointed ERM and CMS to advance environmental and legal work for its proposed 1.5 GW Celtic Sea offshore wind project.
- The development could enter operation in the mid-2030s, supplying renewable electricity to millions of homes.
- The appointments move the project deeper into the UK planning process following its award under The Crown Estate’s Leasing Round 5.
Equinor has appointed environmental consultancy ERM and law firm CMS to support development of its planned 1.5 GW offshore wind project in the Celtic Sea.
The appointments will cover environmental assessment, planning and legal work as the project progresses following its award under The Crown Estate’s Leasing Round 5. A central focus will be preparing the Scoping Report required as part of the site’s lease obligations.
The project, located off South-West England, could become operational in the mid-2030s. At up to 1.5 GW, Equinor says the site has the potential to generate renewable electricity for millions of homes.
Environmental assessment moves forward
ERM will provide planning and environmental consultancy services across the offshore development and its supporting infrastructure.
Its mandate includes an Environmental Impact Assessment scoping exercise and Habitats Regulation Assessment screening. The work will cover the offshore wind farm, transmission cable infrastructure and associated grid connection works.
The Scoping Report is an early but important part of that process. It will seek stakeholder views on the topics and methodologies proposed for inclusion in the project’s Environmental Impact Assessment.
That assessment will feed into the project’s Development Consent Order process. Large offshore wind projects in England and Wales are generally treated as Nationally Significant Infrastructure Projects, placing them within a dedicated planning and consenting framework.
The environmental work therefore extends beyond turbine locations. Cable routes, grid infrastructure, habitats and potential effects on surrounding communities and ecosystems will also form part of the planning process.
Further information on the project will become available through the Planning Inspectorate as the consent process develops.
RELATED ARTICLE: Equinor and bp Bid for Third New York Offshore Wind Solicitation
CMS to steer consent and land strategy
CMS will provide legal and strategic guidance during the project’s pre-application phase. Its role includes supporting Equinor with an application for a Development Consent Order under the Planning Act.
The law firm will also advise on securing the land agreements and rights needed to deliver the development.
Those responsibilities are particularly relevant as offshore wind projects become larger and more closely linked to constraints onshore. Grid connections, cable corridors and land access can affect development schedules even when offshore generation areas have already been secured.
The appointments give Equinor specialist support across both sides of that permitting challenge as it prepares the project for its next development stage.
Celtic Sea emerges as a new offshore wind market
The project is part of a broader push to establish floating offshore wind at commercial scale in the Celtic Sea.
Equinor describes Leasing Round 5 as a “generational opportunity to establish a new offshore wind market in the Celtic Sea, across Wales, South-West England and beyond.”
The Crown Estate process is intended to support a new generation of offshore wind development in waters where floating technology can unlock areas unsuitable for conventional fixed-bottom turbines.
That creates a broader economic question alongside the project’s climate contribution. The development of a Celtic Sea market could generate demand for ports, engineering services, manufacturing, operations and other parts of the offshore wind supply chain.
Equinor says work with local partners is already underway to plan social value initiatives across the region.
For policymakers, the challenge will be turning awarded seabed capacity into operating infrastructure while managing environmental impacts, planning requirements and grid connections. For investors and developers, consenting timelines and infrastructure availability remain critical project risks.
The ERM and CMS appointments place those issues at the centre of Equinor’s next phase. As the Celtic Sea moves from leasing toward development, the success of projects such as Equinor’s 1.5 GW site will help determine how quickly the region can become a meaningful contributor to the UK’s offshore wind and long-term clean power ambitions.

articles.full_text:
Siemens Energy Backs Type One Energy in $200 Million Fusion Raise
- Type One Energy raised $200 million in Series B funding, taking its total capital raised to more than $400 million.
- Siemens Energy Ventures joined the round as Type One works toward commercializing its stellarator fusion technology within a decade.
- The funding will support Infinity One, an engineering prototype in Tennessee designed to validate technology for a future commercial fusion power plant.
Type One Energy has raised $200 million in a Siemens Energy-backed funding round as the US fusion developer moves toward building its first commercial power plant.
The Series B financing brings Type One’s total funding to more than $400 million. It is also the third-largest Series B raise in the fusion sector over the past five years, according to PitchBook data. The company did not disclose its valuation.
Siemens Energy Ventures joined the round alongside new investors Lowercarbon Capital and SiteGround Capital. Existing backers include Bill Gates’ Breakthrough Energy Ventures and Clutterbuck Capital.
The financing puts fresh institutional capital behind one of the fusion industry’s alternative reactor designs. Type One is developing stellarator technology, which uses complex magnetic fields to confine extremely hot plasma.
From fusion research to power plant engineering
Fusion has attracted decades of scientific research because of its potential to provide large volumes of low-carbon electricity. Unlike nuclear fission, fusion combines atomic nuclei rather than splitting them.
Commercial deployment, however, has remained elusive.
That gap is now attracting growing private investment. Advances in magnets, computing and materials have encouraged companies to pursue commercial reactor designs. At the same time, rising electricity demand is increasing pressure to develop new sources of firm, low-carbon power.
Type One is positioning its technology around the stellarator. The company is also working with engineering, construction and industrial partners to shorten development timelines and control costs.
The new capital will support further technology development and deployment of Infinity One, its engineering prototype machine.
Chief Executive Christofer Mowry said the project is focused on proving the design needed for a commercial plant. “It’s not an experimental science project… the only thing that we want to learn is that our design for the fusion machine in the power plant works as advertised.”
Tennessee project targets commercial deployment
Project Infinity is based at Bull Run in Tennessee. Type One plans to use Infinity One to advance the engineering needed for its commercial successor, Infinity Two.
The company hopes to launch Infinity Two within a decade.
That timeline places Type One among a growing group of private fusion companies seeking to move the technology beyond laboratory research and into electricity generation.
The next challenge will be industrial execution. Fusion developers must prove not only that their technology works, but that reactors can be manufactured, financed and operated at commercially viable costs.

Type One aims to work toward a manufacturing partnership with Siemens Energy, potentially giving the start-up access to expertise from one of the world’s major energy technology companies.
Enrique Gonzalez Zanetich, partner at Siemens Energy Ventures, said the investment expands the company’s exposure to emerging fusion technologies. He said the deal strengthened Siemens Energy’s position in fusion “as we continue to explore the technologies and collaborations that can help advance commercialization”.
Fusion moves onto the strategic energy agenda
For investors and energy executives, the Type One financing reflects a broader shift in the fusion market. Capital is increasingly moving toward engineering, supply chains and commercial deployment rather than scientific research alone.
That distinction matters for the power sector.
Electricity demand is rising as economies electrify transport, heating and industry. Data centers and artificial intelligence infrastructure are adding another source of demand. At the same time, governments and companies face pressure to expand low-carbon generation without compromising grid reliability.
Fusion could eventually complement renewables, storage and existing nuclear power by providing firm electricity without operational carbon emissions. Yet substantial technical, regulatory and financing risks remain before commercial deployment can occur at scale.
For Siemens Energy, the investment provides early exposure to a technology that could reshape long-term power generation markets. For Type One, the relationship brings more than capital. Access to industrial manufacturing and energy infrastructure expertise could become critical as fusion companies move from prototypes toward power plants.
The $200 million raise therefore puts Type One into a more consequential phase. The test now is whether stellarator technology can make the transition from promising physics to commercially deployable energy infrastructure.

Applied AI energy company Novele has raised $17 million in an oversubscribed Series A financing as it seeks to turn commercial buildings into flexible energy assets for an increasingly constrained […]

articles.full_text:
Novele Raises $17 Million to Scale AI Energy Platform for Commercial Buildings
- Novele closed an oversubscribed $17 million Series A, led by Boisei Labs, to expand its AI-powered energy management and distributed storage platform.
- The company has engaged more than 2,000 buildings across a 2.6 billion-square-foot pipeline, alongside live deployments with Fortune 50 customers.
- Novele is targeting commercial buildings as a source of grid flexibility as U.S. electricity demand rises from AI infrastructure, data centers and advanced manufacturing.
Applied AI energy company Novele has raised $17 million in an oversubscribed Series A financing as it seeks to turn commercial buildings into flexible energy assets for an increasingly constrained U.S. power grid.
Boisei Labs led the financing. Locke Health, Arup Ventures and national construction firm Barton Malow also participated. The round included several major commercial real estate owners and operators.
Novele will use the capital to expand its engineering, deployment and commercial teams. It also plans to accelerate installations across its active pipeline and further develop BoardOS, its autonomous energy intelligence platform.
The investment comes as U.S. electricity demand begins rising after years of relatively flat growth. Data centers, AI infrastructure and advanced manufacturing are adding substantial new loads. At the same time, transmission infrastructure and new generation capacity can take years to develop.
Novele is betting that part of the solution already exists inside the country’s commercial building stock.
Turning buildings into grid assets
Commercial buildings traditionally operate as passive electricity consumers. Novele’s technology is designed to give building owners greater visibility and control over when and how that electricity is consumed.
Its platform combines BoardOS, an AI-powered energy software system, with EnergyBoard, the company’s distributed energy storage hardware. Together, they create a full-stack energy management system designed for existing and occupied commercial properties.
The technology can analyze energy use, predict demand and reshape building power consumption in real time. For property owners, the potential benefits include lower energy costs, improved resilience and greater control over emissions and energy performance.
“Commercial buildings are among the largest consumers of energy in this country, yet most have remarkably little ability to understand, predict, or control how they use power,” said Charles Conwell, CEO and co-founder of Novele. “As electricity demand accelerates, the grid needs flexibility, and there is an enormous amount of it hiding inside the buildings we already have. Novele gives owners the intelligence and control to unlock it while improving cost, resilience, sustainability, and the tenant experience. We’re building that future with an exceptional team and a group of investors and industry partners who recognized this opportunity early.”
Novele has already secured live deployments with Fortune 50 customers. More than 2,000 buildings are engaged across a pipeline covering 2.6 billion square feet.
The company has also completed large-scale UL 9540A fire testing, supporting its UL 9540 Listing as it prepares for broader deployment.
Investors target grid flexibility
The investment reflects growing interest in technologies that can extract additional flexibility from existing electricity infrastructure.
“Novele represents exactly the kind of technology we believe can create transformative impact at scale,” said George Perry, President and Founder at boisei labs. “Building owners have a clear economic and operational reason to adopt the platform—lower costs, greater resilience, and more intelligent control of their energy, while every deployment also creates a more flexible and efficient electric grid. The striking alignment across customer value, technological innovation, and broader societal benefit is what made Novele such a strongly compelling investment for us.”
Arup Ventures’ involvement also brings engineering expertise to the challenge of deploying distributed energy systems within occupied buildings.
“Distributed energy systems have the potential to play an important role in how buildings and the grid manage growing power demands, but deploying them safely and efficiently in existing buildings requires solving challenges that go well beyond the technology itself,” said Soroush Jalali, Senior Ventures Manager at Arup Ventures. “Our work with Novele is focused on optimizing and streamlining the engineering and deployment process so that safe, distributed energy infrastructure can be deployed more quickly and consistently across the built environment.”
Commercial real estate becomes part of the power system
For building owners, energy management is becoming a financial and operational issue alongside its role in corporate climate strategies. Rising electricity demand, grid constraints and resilience risks are increasing the value of technologies that can manage consumption more dynamically.
Novele’s longer-term strategy goes beyond optimizing individual properties. Networks of buildings capable of actively managing electricity demand could function as distributed energy resources, providing flexibility without waiting for major grid expansion.
That model could give commercial real estate owners a larger role in the energy transition. For utilities and policymakers, it also expands the range of resources available to manage demand growth.
If deployed at scale, the commercial building sector could shift from being primarily a source of electricity demand to becoming an active component of grid management. That shift is gaining relevance as the U.S. confronts the combined power requirements of AI, industrial expansion and broader electrification.

articles.summary:
Zelestra and EDP are expanding their Spanish energy storage partnership with two new power purchase agreements, adding batteries to operational solar plants in Seville and Castilla-La Mancha. The long-term PPAs […]

articles.full_text:
Zelestra, EDP Expand Spain Solar Storage Portfolio Beyond 1 GWh
- Two new PPAs will pair 181 MWdc of operational solar capacity in Spain with approximately 462 MWh of battery storage.
- The Pedroso and Valkyria projects will deploy four-hour battery systems totaling 115.45 MW of power capacity.
- The agreements expand the Zelestra-EDP partnership to four hybrid projects and more than 1 GWh of contracted storage across Spain.
Zelestra and EDP are expanding their Spanish energy storage partnership with two new power purchase agreements, adding batteries to operational solar plants in Seville and Castilla-La Mancha.
The long-term PPAs cover the Pedroso and Valkyria solar projects and will add approximately 462 MWh of battery energy storage. The agreements bring the companies’ Spanish hybrid portfolio to four projects with more than 1 GWh of contracted storage.
The expansion comes as Spain works to increase grid flexibility alongside rapid renewable deployment. For developers and investors, the projects also offer evidence that existing solar assets can support a growing commercial market for battery storage.
Four-hour batteries added to operating solar plants
At Pedroso in Seville, Zelestra will develop a 25 MW battery energy storage system with approximately 100 MWh of capacity. It will operate alongside an existing 31 MWdc solar plant.
The larger Valkyria project in Castilla-La Mancha will combine a 90.45 MW battery system with approximately 362 MWh of storage and 150 MWdc of operational solar.
Both battery systems will have four-hour duration, allowing electricity generated during solar-heavy periods to be shifted into later hours.
EDP is already the offtaker for electricity generated by both solar plants. The new agreements extend that commercial relationship into battery storage as EDP builds its position in Spain’s storage offtake market.
Hybridisation can offer a relatively fast route to adding flexibility to renewable assets. Existing projects already have land, generation infrastructure and grid connections. Adding storage can therefore increase the value and usability of renewable generation without developing an entirely new generation site.
Partnership builds on first Spanish hybrid PPAs
The latest agreements build on two earlier contracts between the companies.
In 2025, Zelestra and EDP signed Spain’s first combined solar and battery storage PPA. That agreement covered 170 MWdc of solar capacity and 400 MWh of storage at Trujillo in Extremadura.
Earlier this year, the companies signed Spain’s first PPA to hybridise an operational solar plant. The project will add a 160 MWh battery system to the 50 MW Pizarroso solar plant in Cáceres.
Across all four projects, the partnership now covers more than 1 GWh of contracted battery storage.
RELATED ARTICLE: Zelestra Starts Operations at First German Solar Plant
Pedro Neves Ferreira, CEO of Global Energy Management at EDP, said: “At EDP, innovation goes beyond deploying renewable generation. We are continuously developing new solutions that combine technology, market expertise and flexibility assets to unlock greater value from clean energy. By integrating storage with renewable generation, we can enhance system resilience, improve efficiency and accelerate the electrification and decarbonisation of the economy.”
Storage becomes a commercial priority
The agreements also point to a wider shift in renewable-energy contracting. As solar penetration increases, developers and offtakers are placing greater value on when renewable electricity reaches the grid, rather than generation volumes alone.
Battery storage can move solar output away from periods of high generation and into evening or early-morning demand. That flexibility can reduce curtailment exposure, support grid stability and create additional commercial value from existing assets.
Jaime Burguete, CEO of Zelestra in Spain, said: “Zelestra and EDP have built something together that is unique in the Spanish market: a commercial partnership that is unlocking large-scale storage capacity that will benefit the wider energy system. These four hybrid projects show that energy storage is bankable in Spain, and we expect this segment of the market to be the main growth area in the years ahead. It also means that every megawatt-hour moved into the evening or early morning is clean power the system would otherwise have had to find elsewhere.”
For investors and energy executives, the portfolio demonstrates how long-term offtake contracts can support storage deployment alongside established renewable assets. As European power systems absorb larger volumes of variable generation, similar hybrid structures could become increasingly important to renewable financing, grid resilience and corporate clean-energy procurement.
